title: Computer-Aided Surgery Arm (ISG Viewing Wand / Raab electrogoniometer, 1988–1993)
subtitle: The surgical pointer that was a counterweighted industrial robot arm: a surgeon's hand became the cursor, and a patient's head became a scrolling 3D model
why_scout_cares: The museum holds plenty of machines that read the body (P300, EEG, EGG) and one that writes into it (the cochlear implant), but nothing from the operating theatre. The ISG Viewing Wand is the clearest 1976–1992 surgical artefact in which the interaction itself is the novelty: the 'pointing device' is not a mouse or light pen but a passive, counterweighted six-axis articulated arm — an electrogoniometer — bolted beside the operating table. The surgeon grips a probe at its free end, touches the patient's scalp to register image space to physical space, and then physically sweeps a meter-long mechanical limb through space while a cursor travels through reformatted CT/MRI slices on a monitor. Feedback is visual only; the arm pushes back against nothing. Simon Raab's 1990 patent drawing (US5251127, public domain) shows the whole apparatus — rolling stand, monitor, articulated links, reference block — with the surgeon standing over the patient, which makes this the rare museum artefact whose primary source image IS the mechanism.

research.title: Computer-Aided Surgery Arm — ISG Viewing Wand
research.by: ISG Technologies Inc. (Toronto / Mississauga, Ontario, Canada); later Elekta Instruments (Atlanta, GA). Core patent inventor: Simon Raab, assigned to FARO Medical Technologies Inc.
research.overview:
The ISG Viewing Wand, sold from roughly 1988–1990 by ISG Technologies of Toronto and in clinical neurosurgical use by 1990–1992, was an intra-operative image-guidance system built around a passive articulated mechanical arm. The surgeon's instrument for talking to the computer was that arm itself: a six-degree-of-freedom, counterbalanced linkage — described in the literature as a 'the proprioceptive robotic-like jointed arm' and as 'a multijointed mechanical arm with a range of a 25 inch radius sphere' — whose joints carried analog/digital hybrid transducers that reported the spatial position of the probe tip.

The workflow was an embodied registration ritual. Before surgery the patient's CT or MRI scans were transferred by magnetic tape from an ISG Allegro workstation to the operating-room unit, which ran on a standard HP Unix workstation. In the theatre the surgeon touched the probe tip to fiducial markers on the patient's scalp, teaching the machine how image coordinates mapped onto the real head. After that, the surgeon simply moved the arm: every sweep of the hand walked a cursor through reformatted axial, coronal and sagittal slices, or through a 3D surface model, so that wherever the physical tip sat in space, a corresponding crosshair sat in the images. In a 17-patient series the system localised lesions to about 1.8 mm (SEM ± 0.36 mm); a 325-case review reported useful registration in 310 of 325 cases (95.4 percent).

The interaction is the museum's subject. There is no camera and no force feedback: the arm is inert, and the only channel back to the surgeon is the picture on the screen. The surgeon is effectively steering a cursor with a metre of metal and a patient's own anatomy as the hard reference surface — a pointing device whose 'screen' is a human head seen through a 3D scan.

deepDive.heading: The pointer is a passive robot arm
deepDive.text: Where the museum's other 1980s inputs are things you hold — a puck, a glove, a light pen, a bat — the Viewing Wand is held *by* the machine and merely guided by the hand. Six joints, each with its own transducer, resolve into a tip position by forward kinematics. Nothing is actuated; the arm does not push back. The resulting feel is of moving a heavy drafting machine through space, with the computer reading out where you went. Simon Raab's 1990 patent (US5251127, filed 31 July 1990, issued 5 October 1993) describes exactly this: patient data developed from a 3D imaging source, instrument position sensed by the articulated linkage, and both converted to signals presented on one video display, so that 'by watching the display' the practitioner can position an instrument.

deepDive.heading: A sterile bag over a robot arm
deepDive.text: The apparatus sat on a rolling stand pushed up beside the operating table, and — because it had to enter a sterile field — the electrogoniometer and its swinging balanced arm were enclosed in a tubular sterile barrier, a bag over the machine. Instruments clipped to the free end were separately autoclave-sterilisable, connecting through a V-block inside the barrier. This is a detail no picture of a workstation screen would ever convey: the surgeon reached into a clear plastic sleeve to move a precision measuring linkage, then clipped a sterilised probe onto its tip.

deepDive.heading: Registration is the first interaction
deepDive.text: The machine knows nothing until it has been taught the patient. The operator touches the probe to fiducial markers placed on the head — or, less accurately, to anatomical landmarks — so that image space and physical space can be lined up. Registration accuracy was the whole game: the 325-case series found fiducial-based registration more accurate than anatomical landmarks, and the system's value depended on the machine being introduced into a procedure 'with minimal additional effort or time … as long as a trained technician performed the data transfer and reconstruction.' The human ritual of pointing at markers is, functionally, the API call that boots the device.

deepDive.heading: A display-only loop in a high-stakes room
deepDive.text: The feedback channel is purely visual: the surgeon watches triplanar 2D slices, with optional 2D/3D views, and adjusts the physical probe accordingly. The system 'helps in surgical planning and interactive surgery,' was used to place minimal craniotomies, localise the tumour–brain interface and excise lesions, and was extended from neurosurgery to otolaryngology for skull-base, cerebello-pontine-angle and temporal-bone work — reportedly over 400 neurosurgical patients at Bristol plus 14 ENT cases. It is a rare museum artefact whose user interface is a single screen in a room that otherwise runs on touch, feel and instruments.

deepDive.heading: Naming traps for the curator
deepDive.text: Three things are commonly conflated and should not be merged. First, the ISG Viewing Wand (ISG Technologies / later Elekta) is not the Douglas or Carl Zeiss 'Viewing Wand' lineage. Second, the ISG Allegro is the separate planning workstation that fed the Viewing Wand images by tape, not the operating-room arm itself. Third, Raab's patent is assigned to FARO Medical Technologies, the medical arm of the Faro Technologies lineage, which licensed or supplied the articulated measurement technology underlying the class of devices — so the patent assignee and the product vendor are different names for adjacent things. The 'electrogoniometer' wording of the patent is the technically accurate description of what the surgeon is actually holding.
